chapter.title: Signed Out
chapter.sub: Twelve rooms stop letting anyone in. The other 277 are on a timer.

items.text: SEASON 3 · EPISODE 1 · DRAFT  Comedy cold open, then a Monday · Sam and Maya · Level L3  Maya's first day at Aldermoor Group: thirty floors, about three hundred meeting rooms, one printer that always wins. At 8:55, twelve rooms stop letting anyone in.  ⚑ RT-03: Aldermoor Group is invented. Identity details are generic (RV-60). Some choices run on a clock — timer settings are in the top bar.

items.title: The Printer Always Wins
items.stakes: Twelve rooms won't let anyone in. The biggest renewal of Renata's quarter is in one of them. The other 277 are on a timer.
items.clock: Four minutes to the pitch. Sixteen hours to 02:00.
items.reward: Every room signs in on Tuesday. Mei's trust, which is harder to earn than a password reset.

objectives.text: Stop Sam typing the password into every panel
Find the timer hidden in twelve failures
Bring Mei something she can approve
Prove it before the fleet restarts
Look closer: two things on day one nobody explains

items.rumor: Rooms break on Mondays. Every Monday. The help desk calls it the Monday Ghost and has stopped laughing about it.

items.alt: An open-plan office in morning light. Sam, in a sky-blue shirt and lanyard, throws up his arms at a printer whose display reads PAPER JAM · TRAY 2. A crumpled sheet sticks out of it.

bubbles.text: Tray two. You don't HAVE a tray two. I've looked. I've been inside you.

items.caption: Sam, IT support. Fast, funny, and on his fourth printer ticket before eight.

lines.text: Tray two. You don't HAVE a tray two. I've been inside you.
(Welcome to corporate AV. It's a lot like church, but the printers are angrier.)

items.alt: The printer now says READY and has produced a test page. Sam grins in triumph. Maya, carrying a cardboard box, stops to watch.

bubbles.text: Test page. It says READY. It's lying, but it's saying it.
Want me to label it?

items.alt: The printer says PAPER JAM · TRAY 2 again. Behind Sam, the IT cupboard door has a yellow sticky note on it: ROOMS PW, and a password written underneath.

bubbles.text: Welcome to Aldermoor. Thirty floors, three hundred rooms, one printer. The printer always wins.
I'm Maya. Priya hired me for the rooms. Not the printer.

items.caption: Nobody's fault. The printer wins. (Look at the cupboard door.)

items.title: A yellow sticky note
items.body: *ROOMS — pw: (redacted by the novel)* — the shared password for every room account in the building, in Sam's handwriting, three years old. It's taped at eye level. It has seen more meetings than anyone.

items.alt: Priya, Aldermoor's network lead, welcomes Maya by her new desk. A pale-blue sticky note on Maya's monitor reads: shared folder — EVERYTHING.

bubbles.text: Three hundred rooms and nobody has ever owned them end to end. Now you do. Good first day.
New laptop, label maker, and every note goes in the shared folder. The last file I kept on one laptop drowned.

items.caption: The rain took her RF plan. She is not doing that twice.

lines.text: New laptop. Label maker. Every note goes in the shared folder.
I'm always thinking about the laptop.

items.alt: Sam points at a whiteboard titled MONDAY GHOST with seven tally marks under 'Mondays in a row'.

bubbles.text: Rooms break on Mondays. Every Monday. Different room, different thing. We call it the Monday Ghost.
Seven Mondays. Has anyone lined them up?

items.caption: Nobody has. Keep the whiteboard in mind.

items.title: Seven Mondays
items.body: Seven dates, seven rooms, seven different causes scribbled beside them. Someone has drawn a small ghost next to each. Under the last one, faint, rubbed half out: *why always Monday??*

items.alt: Sam's phone fills with alerts: Summit can't join, 7-West can't join, and more — twelve rooms in all.

bubbles.text: Twelve rooms won't join calls. TWELVE. On a Monday. Of course on a Monday.
Which twelve? Same floor?

items.alt: Renata, the VP of Sales, stands outside the glass wall of the Summit Room, one hand raised to knock. Inside, the room's touch panel glows red: SIGN-IN FAILED.

bubbles.text: My client is in the lobby. The pitch is at nine. In THAT room. Somebody tell me that room works.

items.caption: The biggest renewal of Renata's quarter (illustrative). Four minutes.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #22 · AVERY'S LENS  Big targets for urgent actions  The more urgent the action, the bigger and closer the target should be (Fitts's law).  At 8:56 a stressed presenter needs a huge JOIN button, not a menu.

items.alt: Close on the Summit Room panel's info screen: Room unavailable. Account sign-in failed: password expired. Ring: PILOT. Last restart: Sunday 02:00. Sam points at it.

bubbles.text: Pilot rooms. Updates hit them first, Sunday at two. The other two hundred and seventy-seven restart Monday night.

items.caption: Read the screen before you touch the room.

items.prompt: 8:56. The client is walking in. The Summit Room won't join the call. Decide.
items.happening: The Summit Room shows SIGN-IN FAILED. The client is in the lift.
known: ◉ The table input works without the room account
unknown: Why the rooms can't sign in
items.risk: Renata's client, and the first impression Aldermoor makes today.
timeout: The client sits down in a room with a red panel and a VP apologizing. Renata starts the pitch on her phone.
Not deciding is a decision. The laptop fallback was the whole answer for the next hour.

hints.text: Contain first. What in that room works without the room signing in?
A laptop on the table input doesn't need the room account.

options.label: Walk the client to a working room on floor 4
options.result: Floor 4's only free room seats six. There are nine people. They stand for the first ten minutes.
options.consequence: It works, badly, and the client notices the scramble.

options.label: Restart the Summit Room
options.result: Four minutes of a black screen. It comes back, tries the same expired password, and fails again.
options.consequence: The pitch starts late and the panel's sign-in record from Sunday is gone.
options.fail: A restart is what caused this. You repeated it in front of the client and erased the panel's record.

options.label: Renata joins from her laptop on the table input
options.result: Laptop on the table cable; the room display and speakers take it. Slides and faces at 9:01.
options.consequence: The client never knows. The broken panel stays exactly as it was, for you to read.

options.label: Call the conferencing vendor's support line
options.result: Hold music. “Your call is important to us.”
options.consequence: Nine o'clock arrives in the queue.
options.fail: Escalation is right when you can't contain it yourself. Here the fallback was on the table.

items.alt: Inside the Summit Room: the display shows the client and Renata as video tiles above a slide that reads Q3 PROPOSAL. A laptop sits on the table.
items.caption: 9:01. The pitch runs from a laptop. The client never knows.

items.text: 🔭 PHYSICS IN MOTION  How strong is a room password?  The science under this episode’s problem — live.

items.sub: Beginner · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Mei and Maya beside a board. A shared account is one login for many people. A named account is one person's. Password entropy is how unpredictable a password is, in bits. How do you count bits? Length times log-two of the symbols. Twelve random lowercase letters: twelve times log-two of twenty-six — about fifty-six bits. Length wins.

bubbles.text: A shared account is one login for many people. A named account is one person's. Password entropy is how unpredictable a password is, in bits.
How do you count bits?
Length times log-two of the symbols. Twelve random lowercase letters: twelve times log-two of twenty-six — about fifty-six bits. Length wins.

items.caption: Beginner: the term, what it means, the formula — and one worked example out loud.

items.text: 📘 RAY'S NOTEBOOK · BEGINNER  Terms    Password entropy   How unpredictable a password is, in bits.   Shared account   One login used by many people — impossible to trace or revoke for one person.   Named account   A login for one person, with only the access they need.   Formula, variables and a worked example   ƒ FORMULA · Password entropy  H = L × log 2 (N)   H  entropy, bits  L  length, characters  N  size of the symbol set    Worked example.  A 12-character password from 26 lowercase letters: 12 × log₂(26) ≈ 56 bits.

📒 EMPATHIA LEARN FIELDBOOK · MODULE 22 OF 31 · PP. 10–25  PART 1 CORE TECHNOLOGY FOUNDATIONS  On Avery's first day at Aldermoor, Maya photocopied page 11 for her. At the top she wrote: “Accounts are part of the system. — M.”

items.label: **Fieldbook module 22 — Computers in AV — accounts, updates and habits.** Beginner support: every new word is defined, and every formula comes with its variables and a worked example.

items.alt: Outside room 7-West, Sam stands at another red panel, ready to type. Maya stops him with an open hand.

bubbles.text: I know the room password. I'll just sign them back in. Twelve rooms, twelve minutes.
Twelve rooms, same minute, same error. That isn't twelve problems.

items.prompt: I know the room password. Twelve rooms, twelve minutes. Why are you looking at me like that?

options.label: “Twelve rooms, same minute, same error. That's one problem. Let's find it first.”
options.reply: …Okay. That's annoyingly reasonable. Where do we look?

options.label: “Go on, then.”
options.reply: Please don't. I'm two floors down and I type fast.

options.label: “Is that password on a sticky note?”

items.prompt: 9:04. Sam is about to type the room password into every panel. What do you do?
items.happening: Twelve rooms, one error: password expired.
known: ◉ All twelve: ring PILOT, restarted Sun 02:00
items.risk: Every meeting booked in those rooms this morning — and the accounts' security.
timeout: Sam, trying to help, types the password into 7-West and hits “choose a new password”. He freezes with his fingers on the keys.
Under pressure, an idle plan gets replaced by the nearest button.

hints.text: Twelve at once is a pattern. Patterns have one cause.
Whose accounts are these? Not Sam's, and not yours.

options.label: Let Sam work through all twelve
options.result: 7-West: “Password expired — choose a new password.” Sam hesitates. 18-North locks after three tries.
options.consequence: Now two rooms are locked out and Sam is about to invent a new secret for an account he doesn't own.
options.fail: Typing a password into a policy prompt means choosing a new credential for an account security owns — one room at a time.

options.label: Stop. Find what the twelve have in common first
options.result: Maya lists them: six floors, five switches, one identical error, all in the pilot ring. A personal laptop joins fine from 7-West.
options.consequence: Ten minutes of looking narrows it to identity — and to whose it is.

options.label: Reset the room accounts from Sam's help-desk console
options.result: The console lets him. That's the problem: it would set one new password across the rooms, chosen by Sam.
options.consequence: Mei would learn about it from the audit log.
options.fail: Having the button isn't having the authority. Room accounts belong to the identity team; access decisions belong to security.

options.label: Restart all twelve rooms together
options.result: Twelve rooms go dark for four minutes and come back with the same error.
options.consequence: Every panel's sign-in record is gone.
options.fail: Twelve restarts repeat the cause twelve times.

items.alt: Maya's notebook: twelve rooms, six floors, five switches, all 'password expired', all ring PILOT restarted Sunday 2 a.m.; a laptop in 7-West joins fine; so not network, not service — accounts. Whose?
items.caption: Different floors, different switches, one error. The network didn't do this.

items.label: **Clue Board:** twelve rooms, one cause. Which clues separate the explanations?

items.alt: Mei, a security analyst in graphite and indigo with glasses and a lanyard, arrives at a brisk walk.

bubbles.text: You're the new AV engineer. Please don't reset anything on those room accounts.
I wasn't going to. Whose are they?

items.caption: Mei · security analyst. Precise, not cold.

items.alt: Mei shows Friday's change record on a tablet: passwords older than 90 days must change at next sign-in; scope default account policy; impacted staff from the people directory; rooms not listed.

bubbles.text: Friday's change. It closes an audit finding. Room accounts sit in the default policy — and the record never listed them.

items.caption: The record exists. It was built from a list of people. Rooms aren't people.

items.alt: System View: a restarted room computer signs in to the identity service; Friday's policy sees a password 912 days old and demands a new one; a room can't type, so it is signed out. Laptops belonging to people sign in fine.
items.caption: Symptom: Control (the room won't join). Cause: Dependency (identity).

items.alt: Maya rubs the back of her neck. Mei answers without a trace of impatience.

bubbles.text: Identity isn't my world. Last month I was coordinating radio mics in a field.
Evidence is your world. You just walked me from a red panel to Friday's change in twenty minutes.

lines.text: Identity isn't my world. Last month I was coordinating radio mics in a field.
Also, nobody in this building knows how radio mics work. Keep that quiet. It's leverage.

items.label: **Learn it now:** identity and room accounts — why a policy for people can sign a room out.

items.alt: Maya and Sam, faces lit by the same thought. Two labels hang between them: pilot ring restarted Sunday 2 a.m.; fleet restarts tonight 2 a.m.

bubbles.text: The twelve failed because they restarted. The rest haven't signed in since Friday. They're not fine. They just haven't been asked yet.
Tonight at two. All two hundred and seventy-seven. Every room in the building.

items.title: It isn't twelve rooms. It's all of them — on a timer.
items.body: The pilot rooms weren't unlucky; they were first. Every room account in the default policy has a password older than ninety days. The rest of the fleet is still signed in only because it hasn't restarted since Friday. At 02:00 it does.
items.label: Test: reason from the new fact before you read on.

items.alt: The operations corner: a wall of status tiles. A red label reads 02:00 → 277 rooms restart. Priya is on the phone; Maya waits.

bubbles.text: Tuesday morning, every room in the building asks for a new password. And a room can't type.
Then it gets fixed before two. Properly, by the people who own it.

items.prompt: It's 10:30. You have until 02:00. What do you bring to Mei?
items.happening: 277 rooms will fail at 02:00 unless the room accounts change.
known: ▮ Password age on the room accounts: up to 912 days
unknown: What the identity team can change today
items.risk: Every meeting in the building tomorrow morning.

options.label: A request to roll the policy back until rooms are sorted
options.result: Mei: “That closes an audit finding. Tell me what broke, not what to undo.”
options.consequence: An hour spent arguing about the wrong thing.
options.fail: You asked security to re-open a risk to fix a symptom.

options.label: An evidence pack: which rooms, the error, the ring and restart times, Friday's change — and a verification plan
options.result: Mei reads it in two minutes. “My team can move room accounts to a room-account policy today. You prove the rooms.”
options.consequence: The owner decides; you bring facts and a way to prove the result.

options.label: Turn off the nightly restarts fleet-wide
options.result: No room signs in tonight. No room takes tonight's security updates either.
options.consequence: The time bomb is still there, one restart away, now unpatched.
options.fail: You hid the trigger instead of fixing the cause, and stopped security updates to do it.

options.label: Exempt the room accounts from password policy yourself
options.consequence: Mei finds out from the audit log at 11:02.
options.fail: Exempting accounts from a security policy is an access decision. It isn't yours.

items.title: Shannon on secrecy
items.body: In 1949 Claude Shannon published the mathematics of secret communication, treating a key's strength as the number of possibilities an attacker must try. Every password policy that locked twelve rooms out on a Monday is a descendant.

items.alt: Renata, back from her pitch, confronts Sam at his desk.

bubbles.text: Just roll the password thing back. Security broke the rooms. Security can un-break them.
That's… honestly what I'd do.

items.alt: Mei holds up an audit report excerpt: Finding 7 — one password for every meeting-room account, unchanged three years, found written on a note on the IT cupboard, floor 12. A photo of the sticky note is pinned to it.

bubbles.text: The policy exists because of this. One password, every room, three years, taped to a door.

items.caption: The note from the cold open. Every camera, microphone and calendar in the building, one key.

items.alt: Sam stands by the IT cupboard, eyes closed. The sticky note is gone from the door. Maya watches him.

bubbles.text: That's my note. Night shift kept getting locked out of rooms. It was supposed to be for a week.
Temporary is the longest-lasting thing in any building.

lines.text: That's my note. Night shift kept getting locked out. It was supposed to be for a week.
Temporary is the longest-lasting thing in any building.

items.title: The outage is the policy working. The hole is the note.
items.body: Security didn't break the rooms; the rooms were already broken — every one of them opened by the same secret, written on a door, for three years. Rolling back fixes Monday and re-opens the finding. The fix has to remove both problems at once.
items.label: Test: given the audit photo, what's the right fix — and whose is it?

items.alt: Mei, to Sam, gently.

bubbles.text: Nobody's in trouble for a sticky note. We'd be in trouble for putting it back.
…Okay. What do you need from me?

items.alt: A screen: identity team change complete — room accounts moved: 289; room-account policy; unique credentials per room; rotation managed by the identity team; sign-in limited to the room device; completed 16:48.
items.caption: 289 room accounts. The badge says about three hundred rooms. Nobody does the subtraction today.

items.title: “~300 rooms”
items.body: The account list has 289. The badge says about three hundred. Maya writes 289 in her log and never does the subtraction. Eleven is a small number. It's also a whole floor.

items.prompt: 16:50. The change is in. The fleet restarts at 02:00. How do you prove it first?
items.happening: 289 room accounts moved to the room-account policy.
known: ◉ Twelve pilot rooms are known and already broken
unknown: Whether a room signs in with the new credential
timeout: Everyone goes home. At 02:00 the fleet restarts on an untested change.
Nobody deciding is the same as choosing option A.

hints.text: Prove it where it's safe first: rooms that are already broken.

options.label: Wait for the morning and see
options.result: At 8:55 you'll know. So will everyone in 277 rooms.
options.fail: If the change is wrong, you find out when every meeting in the building does.

options.label: Restart the twelve pilot rooms now and make a real call from one
options.result: Twelve panels restart, sign in, show READY. Sam calls Maya's phone on cellular from the Summit Room: picture, voice, slides.
options.consequence: A small, known ring proves it before the fleet depends on it.

options.label: Restart all 289 rooms right now
options.result: Every room in the building goes dark at 4:50 p.m., including three live meetings.
options.consequence: If the change is wrong, you've broken the fleet yourself, at once.
options.fail: Never test on everyone at once, and never during business hours.

options.label: Trust the identity team's “complete” message
options.result: It is complete — as a change. Nobody has watched a room sign in yet.
options.consequence: A change record isn't a working room.

items.alt: Two pilot-room panels glow green: READY. Sam is on the Summit Room's call; Maya's phone, on cellular, shows the Summit Room with checkmarks for voice, video and slides.

bubbles.text: Summit calling the new engineer. On cellular, outside our network. Do you see my slides?

items.caption: Proof where the people are: a real call to a far end on a network that isn't ours.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run 8:55 Monday yourself — the pitch, the twelve rooms, and the 02:00 clock.

items.alt: Tuesday morning at the operations wall: a green label reads 02:00 — 277 restarts, zero sign-in failures. Sam holds a coffee aloft.

bubbles.text: Two hundred seventy-seven restarts. Zero failures. I want it on a mug.
Walk three rooms at 8:30, when there are people in them. Then the mug.

items.label: **Sequence:** put the day's work in order — from 8:55 to the 02:00 restart.

items.alt: Maya's first change-log entry at Aldermoor: Monday, 12 pilot rooms signed out; Friday's password-age policy hit room accounts; identity team moved 289 room accounts to a room policy with unique, rotated credentials; proof on the pilot ring and a real call, fleet zero failures; change template must list room accounts; sticky note shredded with Mei watching; owners Mei for identity, Maya for rooms.
Late afternoon. Mei stops by Maya's desk on her way out.

bubbles.text: You never touched the accounts. Not once, all day.
Not mine. The rooms are. I'll tell you the second one of them does something strange.

items.alt: Back at the printer, still jammed. Maya has stuck a printed label on its side: NO TRAY 2. EVER. Sam grins.

bubbles.text: Did the label fix it?
No. But now it's honest.

items.caption: The printer still wins. It just can't lie about it.

items.alt: Sam at his desk, reading a new ticket on his monitor: Harbor Room, priority 2. A remote participant writes: I can hear myself in the Harbor Room. Only the Harbor Room.

bubbles.text: Maya? You're going to like this one. It's got an echo.

items.caption: Next: *The Room That Hears Twice.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A meeting room signs in like a person, and a policy written for people can sign it out. When many rooms fail at once, look for the one thing they share before touching any of them. Contain with a fallback that doesn't need the broken part, bring evidence to the owner of the account, let them make the access change, then prove it on a small ring with a real call before the whole fleet relies on it.

REFLECTION (optional)  · Sam's note was kindness to the night shift, and it quietly became the biggest risk in the building. What 'temporary' thing in your own work has outlived its week?  Boundary: this reflection doesn't prove anything about the rooms.
